column2: And this. Someone near the ration station asked me to bring it for a valuation. Don't buy it yet. Appraise it. I want to hear what you'd quote too.
Tool awaiting appraisal
You've already written that one up. Don't do it twice just to hear another compliment.
That's enough appraising for now. While you were looking at it, something else came to mind.
The locket needs a 2×2 space. Existing items are preserved; move it into room and its shape will be updated.
Each item is priced separately. Bargain or pass; we can still talk.
Leave the order. I'll see what I can prepare.
That's the business noted. There's something just for you, too.
That's the budget spent. Everything collected is paid for. I'll find another way to source the rest.
Here for the tools-and-materials order. I've collected {0} tools and {1} materials; {2} credits remain. Show me what you have. We settle each purchase as we go.
I'll pass this time. Don't let me hold up your search.
That's everything. Goods collected, accounts settled. Don't look so surprised. I really did come to give you some business.
The tools-and-materials order has closed. Delivered goods were paid for; the remaining supplies will be sourced elsewhere.
Mother asked me to bring a small request too. Decide whether you want it. Don't say yes just because I brought it.

Two working tools and one ordinary material item. Six hundred in buying funds; we'll inspect and price the goods together. I'll come in two days. If you're short then, you've another four days. Don't empty your own shelves for it.
I'll take these. I'll ask about the rest in two days. Don't buy bad goods just to finish the order.
Interested in the order?

2 tool items and 1 material item. Total buying funds: 600; prices negotiated and paid on delivery. Due four days after the first collection visit. Declining or missing it does not change the relationship or rescue.
Proper business today. They need tools, materials and household goods upstairs. I'm buying for them, with nine hundred to spend. Goods first. I'll tell you about the launch afterwards.
I'm bringing something for a valuation today. Relax. They want to know what the item is worth, not how much your young lady has spent.
Some people near the ration station pooled money for tools and household goods. Quote normally. Don't give up your margin just because it's me.
All right, that's enough for today. The shop keeps opening; I keep getting on with life. We can deal with Wilde when we're ready.
Two items. My own goods; separate payment. Look them over. I promise the labels survived this time.
Keep it safe. And don't put that one on today's bill.
A sample from Eleanor's first order. Tip, grip and provenance checked. Already covered by the preparations; no further charge.
I'll keep the sample for you. Not taking stock doesn't stop me delivering my own order.
You haven't taken that sample yet. Room on the counter today? It's free. Don't start bargaining with me again.
Let's see the materials.
No stock this time. Tell me about upstairs.
I asked about two small lots on the way: tools or materials. Didn't commit you to either. Want a look? The pass and clothes are paid for. These goods are a separate purchase.
Which lot this time?
The lot you chose is still here. Don't rush. It hasn't grown legs.
Show me the tools.
Here. Look them over. We can take our time with the price.
Take the crate and put it on the counter.
You can inspect it later, or hand it to her directly.
Accept it.
She has started noticing what you need.
Take it, but inspect the crate first.
The stolen-goods record will show up. It may also draw attention.
I'll take them. It's compensation for the negotiation.
Taking the money doesn't mean you've priced her mother.
Give it to you and your mother for living costs.
You don't keep the money; it should go to the people who need it.
I won't take it.
You don't want this to look like a sale.
I care about you. But not that way.
Friends route; the rescue is not undone.
I want to know you better. Can we take it slower?
No affection penalty; one more confirmation later.
I like you too. It has nothing to do with where you used to live.
Accept her feelings clearly.
You keep it. It is safer with you.
She holds the drive; you cannot sell it behind her back.
This is too much. I can't be involved anymore.
The line ends here. She will not trust you with anything important again.
Leave it with me. No one takes it without asking you first.
You become the custodian; only you can hand it over.
I want you to come here as more than a regular.
Confirm the 'slower' answer from before.
I've thought it through. Let's stay friends.
Choose friendship, ending the deferred romance decision.
Take the pheromone perfume.
An upper-district item. It might fetch a good price down here.
Take the portable water purifier.
She insists on thanking you. This one will last a while.
Do not mention the crate yet.
She will not know the danger; the trap remains armed.
Keep it. You need it more.
She still has an investigator to pay. Remember the thought.
Pay the normal price.
You do not want her gift to become another debt.
Use the slower ordinary review (cost {0} credits)
Requires a record from successfully exposing the fake uncle.
If it cannot be done, switch to the exchange.
Keeping her mother alive comes first.
Use a Security review and temporary custody (Security rep {0}+, cost {1} credits)
Requires an existing frame-up or threat record.
Ask the upper district for named sponsorship (Upper District rep {0}+, cost {1} credits)
Trade the work log for acceptance. This is not buying a verdict.
Refuse and let him take it away.
If she never receives it, the trap cannot spring.
Keep it and sell it.
She is still saving for the investigator.
It looks better on you. I'll take the thought.
The locket stays with her.
Go back and raise the money. Return tomorrow.
She is still inside. You are not done trying.
Bring your mother back first. Return the research.
An exchange. Mother and daughter can reunite below, but the research is not published.
Secure the transfer and protection first. Decide who receives the research after she is safe.
Requires admissible material and a channel that actually responds.
Publish the research now.
She takes part in the decision, but no one can promise her mother will live.
This is too much. I'm stepping away.
A normal exit; she handles the rest herself.
Let her finish the investigation herself.
She earned the money. The decision is hers too.
Offer money in exchange for control (cost {0} credits)
She will refuse. Some things are not debts.
Give the drive to a newspaper without telling her.
You make this decision for her, behind her back.
Then I'll keep it.
Accept her gift.
Tell her about the crate.
Let her know it was reported stolen, and not to touch it.
Hand him the drive and take the three hundred (+{0})
Deciding behind her back puts a price on her mother. The relationship ends.
Just make him leave.
Remember the offer and tell her next time. The threat remains.
Hand the record to Security (Security rep {0}+)
Requires an existing frame-up or threat record, and a channel that actually responds.
Sell the drive to a black-market buyer (+{0})
They promise nothing about her mother. The research leaves both your hands.
Ask the upper district to make contact (Upper District rep {0}+)
Trade the research work log for a verifiable response.

The continuing supply contracts are settled too. From tomorrow your share is 600 credits a day. The earlier accounts still stand. Don't call it paying back my wages. This is business we built together.

Once the first order is settled, a share goes to you. From tomorrow, I'll set aside 200 credits a day and bring it when I visit. Missing a visit won't lose you anything. Your capital and the goods we checked together are part of this business.
After the business opens, daily dividends rise to 600 credits, paid during visits.
After the first order succeeds, 200 credits accrue daily, paid during Eleanor's visits.
Here's your share: {0} credits. Everything set aside up to today. Count it. Don't look at me like that. My accounts aren't missing a line.
Keep it safe. I'll keep recording the rest and settle it next time I come.
Eleanor's dividend received: {0} credits. Still awaiting collection: {1}.
Dividends: {0}/day; awaiting collection {1}; received in total {2}.
Brought the accounts. Let's check these entries first. We can talk goods afterwards.
Both referrals went through. Lydia's plaque is bringing in more Upper Level customers.
I'll take it. She recommended the right place.
Lydia sent me. I heard you have something fine enough for the Upper Levels. My budget today is about {0} credits. If it suits, I'll buy it the usual way.
Nothing suitable today. I'll come back another time.
This will do. Worth the trip.
Lydia said you can find a portable water purifier. Budget {0} credits, at least {1} durability. Show me the item first; we'll negotiate the price normally.
If there's nothing suitable, never mind. Lydia said I can ask again here.
Starts Lydia's matchmaking help. Does not mean accepting a two-person romance; no fee.
I do like her. Tell me. I'm listening.
Continue the original ordinary romance route; this expansion does not begin. Refusal does not lower affection.
I want to tell her how I feel myself.
Receive the unique recommendation plaque. The player places it in the showcase to enable referrals. No route fee; does not commit to a two-person romance.
I'll take it. I'll treat the customers you send well.
Not taken and not active. It can be collected once during a later safe visit from Lydia. She will not keep pushing, and it does not affect matchmaking or romance.
Hold the plaque for me for now. I'm not ready with the stock.
(Say it) I like you.
(Hold back) Let me think it through, then I'll tell you.
(Be clear) I care about you, but let's stay friends.
Book a real buyer to visit no earlier than the next business day. Show a clear budget and item requirements. No upfront fee and no guarantee of a sale.
Ask her to come on the next business day, and I'll show her what's suitable.
No booking this time. You can ask again through an existing business opportunity later. Not completing it does not block the romance main line.
I don't have anything suitable. Don't make her waste the trip.
Both options only affect her response. Neither establishes romance or locks the later dual romance; the actual branching happens in Chapter 14.
I think Eleanor has one just like it.
Both options only affect her response. Neither establishes romance or locks the later dual romance; the actual branching happens in Chapter 14.
It suits you.
Open the explicit three-way discussion; nothing is committed yet.
I like you too. But I'm with her, and I won't promise you anything behind her back. I'll tell her this myself.
Continue the three-way discussion; nothing is committed yet.
I won't promise behind her back. Let's tell her together.
Keep the discussion going and keep meeting as usual.
I need a little time, but I'm not backing out.
Continue the joint discussion; the relationship is not registered yet.
All right. After you two talk. Whatever you want to ask me, I'll answer.
Commit the dual relationship after both explicit agreements; no fee.
If you're both willing too, then starting today, let's be serious about this—all three of us.
Come here. Let me hold you for a while.
Sit closer. Let's take our time talking today.
Enter the legacy-save matchmaking and recommendation content. The original confession is not replayed, and no fee is charged.
All right. You come up with ideas, and I'll ask her myself.
Decline this expansion. It will not be pushed again, and the original ordinary romance continues.
We'll arrange it ourselves. When you come to the shop, sit down as usual.
...So this is what you look like. Her description was completely off.
How did she describe me?
Not telling you. You'd get a big head.
She wasn't always like this. She used to ask me which dress to wear before she went anywhere.
And now?
Now she won't even take a job I found for her. ...Never mind. I'll say that to her myself.
*She pauses in the doorway, looking first at the person behind the counter, then at the counter itself. Her half-tied long curls slip over her shoulder, and she brushes them aside.*
Did you come to sell something, or to test me?
...Both. I wanted to see whether you'd take a bargain when it walks through your door.
Done testing?
Done. Don't tell her about this. She'd definitely call me a busybody.
So this is the shop Eleanor never stops talking about?
She's not here today.
I know. I picked a time when she wouldn't be here.
Buying or selling?
Selling. *sets a bracelet on the counter* I'll name a price. You decide what you're willing to pay.
She says you have a sharp eye. I'd like to see how sharp.
There was a pattern on the box she kept the bracelet in. I've seen it on shipment manifests from upstairs.
It's her family's. They're one of the Upper Level families that sell household goods, perfume, and fabric.
No wonder her price felt like a test.
When she was growing up, shop assistants always asked whether she liked something before anything else. Here, she wanted to see what happens when no one's flattering her.
Her family's business is so big. When your family ran into trouble...
Her family sells perfume and bedsheets. They don't run the courts.
...All she could do was come down to see me every few days. Of all those friends upstairs, she's the only one who still bothers.
She does care about you.
She cares. She just always wants to pick the whole road for me.
Good! Rule one: if she isn't in a hurry to leave, whatever you do, don't ask 'What else do you have?' Just say—your hair clip looks nice today.
What if she isn't wearing a hair clip that day?
Then compliment something else! ...It's not about the hair clip. You have to look at her, not just the counter.
How long did you prepare all this?
Not long. Just... a few lines. They work! Don't laugh. Thank me after you've used them.
Fine, I'll stay out of it. ...But if she asks, I'll say you finally said something decent today.
There's something else. She brings you up more often than she talks about how much she made today.
Probably complaining about me.
Of course she's complaining! She can't admit she misses you every time she sees me.
Did she send you?
If she knew I came, she'd strangle me.
So I'll just say it—if you really like her, I can give you a hand.
Why?
Because she's my friend. And because every time she tells me what you two talked about, it always ends up being about prices! Listening to you two stresses me out.
No tests today. I came to say thanks.
For what?
Since her mother came back, she's finally willing to get some proper sleep. I went to see her the day before yesterday, and she actually slept until noon.
She held on for a long time.
Yeah. I used to tell her to go back upstairs and find someone she knew to smooth things over. She wouldn't listen, and I even got angry at her.
Looking back, while she was going through the worst of it, I was still telling her which dress made her look lively. ...I wasn't hearing a word she was saying.
Have you told her all this?
I did. She cursed me out a little, then asked if I'd eaten. I think that counts as forgiveness.
Your name's already engraved on it. It ought to be seen.
...You make it sound like I've put myself up as collateral here.
Isn't the plaque worth a meal?
It is! Once the business works out, I'll pick the place.
Fine, I'll keep it for you. Tell me when you're ready. Don't get shy about asking when the time comes.
When have I ever been shy about taking in goods?
...Fair point.
We're agreed, all right? When Eleanor comes, don't open your mouth with how many extra customers you had today.
Who was just drumming up business for me?
I bring in the business and teach you what to say. At least remember half of it!
Nothing suitable today. I do have ordinary household goods, but don't recommend the wrong thing.
Then I won't make her come for nothing. I know a few shops that sometimes clear out unused older stock. I'll have some sent over next time. You look first, and you decide whether to take it.
We'll discuss the price as usual.
I know, I know. You haven't even seen the goods, and I'm already saying it for you.
*After saying her piece, Lydia doesn't get up. Her gaze drifts to the showcase.*
Oh, right—do you have any decent household goods? Skin care, water purification... Don't rush to say no. I think I caught sight of something just now.
Who's it for? Tell me the use first.
Not me. I know a lady who keeps complaining that the shop she frequents bundles everything together. She wants one thing, and the clerks insist on showing her a whole set.
Here you can discuss one item at a time.
She'll like hearing that.

*At last she opens her small bag and takes out a tiny enamel recommendation plaque. Its base is polished bright, the edge bears the pattern you've seen on the shipment manifests, and a name is engraved on its own line below.*
Put this in the showcase. Don't shove it under the counter.
Your family's sign?
The pattern is my family's. The line below is my name. Anyone who recognizes it will know this is a shop that I, Lydia, am willing to speak up for.
Decided to vouch for me that quickly?
It's not like I met you today. That business with the bracelet... never mind, I was in the wrong that time. I've been watching how you helped her since then.
Helping her and being good at business are two different things.
So I've been watching your business too! Didn't you just spend ages asking me what it was for?
*She pushes the plaque toward your hand, then reaches out to straighten its slightly crooked base.*
I can get them to walk through the door. Whether you can keep them once they're inside is up to you.
I can do that.
Then put it out. Next time I come, I want to see it from outside.
You can show her this one. Whether it suits her, we'll see once she looks at it.
You won't even say 'I guarantee she'll be satisfied' first?
She hasn't even come yet. Who am I guaranteeing satisfaction for?
...Fair. Some shops upstairs hear my family name and say it's definitely suitable before I've even finished asking.
Is your family name really that useful?
Plenty of people recognize it. I used to think it was convenient. Then I'd buy something that didn't work, take it back, and every one of them remembered that I was the one who'd nodded.
So this time you ask first.
Right. And she's coming to you to buy something, not to my family.
She said she wants to send customers your way.
First I need the stock ready.
Mm. When she gets enthusiastic, she runs ahead. Just tell her clearly what you can actually do.
That's everything for today. The money's right.
Mm.
*'What else do you have?' is already on your tongue. You swallow it back.*
You... look well today.
I slept three hours last night.
Lydia came by, didn't she?
She did.
Did she teach you that?
A few lines. She told me not to open with asking what else you have.
She really will teach anything!
But asking you to stay a little longer was my own idea.
...That's more like it.
*She glances at the door, then sets the bag she'd already picked up back down by her feet.*
How's your mother today?
She complained that I'd put everything away too neatly and now she can't find anything. Then she shooed me out and told me to find something of my own to do.
So you came here?
To sell goods! ...And to sit for a while.
That plaque... She gave you even that?
She said she'd send customers my way.
When she likes a shop, she can sing its praises for ages. But she's only put her own name out like that a handful of times.
Should I thank her for you?
Thank her yourself. Not everything has to go through me.
*She digs a folded piece of paper out of her small bag. On it is a drawing of a flower-shaped brooch, with a price beside it crossed out and rewritten twice.*
I've got my eye on an old brooch. The shopkeeper says some famous person wore it, but I just think the petals are beautifully made. Is the extra price worth it?
Where is it?
Still in the shop. I haven't paid. I wanted to ask you first. ...Don't laugh at me for only caring whether something looks good.
Looking good is a reason. As for who wore it, he needs to show proof. I haven't seen the item, so I won't price it for you.
So it's not that I don't know how to appreciate it—it's that I don't have to pay for the story too?
Right. If you like the petals, negotiate on the price of the petals.
I thought you'd say this kind of thing is useless.
If you like it, it's useful. You don't need to pay extra for a nice story.
*She folds the paper and is about to ask something else when her stomach gives a soft rumble. She glances down and pretends to straighten her skirt.*
You haven't eaten today?
...I came to teach you how to care about her, and you're practicing on me first.
That needs practice?
I'll just—
A piece of dessert later counts as lunch? Eat something proper first.
*She looks at you for a moment, then finally gives a slightly embarrassed smile.*
...All right. I won't pass this one on to her.
Every time you come, you ask about her first, then about customers. What about you?
Me...? There's actually something I'm not sure about.
She said she didn't buy anything today. I thought you two had argued. When I asked, it turned out she just didn't find the right thing.
A deal falling through doesn't mean we argued.
I know. She also said you didn't pressure her. Next time I'll ask exactly what she wants first, so she doesn't make a wasted trip.
How's the stock coming along? If it's not ready, don't give me a random date. I'll take it seriously and tell people.
When it's ready, I'll say so myself.
Good, I won't push today. ...Actually, I came today because I wanted to ask about something of my own.
She got back to me! She said the purchase was clear and you didn't push a pile of useless things on her.
You sent her, and I did business as usual.
As usual is exactly right. If you were extra polite just for her, I'd be afraid to bring anyone next time.
And now you dare?
I do. On my way here, I even took a look at my name in the showcase.
Then I'll say it. I like you. I don't want to be just the shopkeeper you come to when something's wrong.
*She looks at you, and the retort she had ready never comes out.*
...Did she teach you that too?
She only taught me to say it clearly. Who I like doesn't need her teaching.
...Me too.
Me too, which part?
That I like you! Did you hear me clearly?
Clearly. I won't make you guess anymore.
*You hold out your hand. She looks at it, then places her hand in yours.*
There's still dust on my hand.
Should I let go?
Who told you to let go?
It's not that I don't want to say it. I want to say it once I've thought it through.
Then when you've thought it through, come tell me yourself. Don't have Lydia pass messages for you again.
...I understand.
We'll keep doing business. Don't start avoiding me just because we've had this talk.
Everyone I see lately asks what I'm going to do next.
What are you going to do?
Live a good life. Find a proper job, take care of my mother. ...And sometimes, I want to come here.
Only sometimes?
Do you have to pick apart every single word!
She really thinks I can't tell.
Should I call her back?
...Move your glass this way. It's in the way over there.
*She pushes the empty chair in and sits a little closer to you.*
*Halfway through the meal, Lydia checks the time and sets down her glass.*
Oh no, I promised to meet someone about clothes! Take your time. No need to walk me out.
Didn't you just say that shop closes early today?
...There's another shop! Anyway, take your time!
*She leaves too quickly, then comes back for the shawl she left on the chair. As she passes you, she lowers her voice.*
Don't just talk about goods again.
I booked a table for three. She's been so busy she barely eats. It's a good excuse to drag her out.
You're coming too?
Of course! Otherwise you two would sit there staring at each other. Who'd make conversation?
Good. I'll only tell her you're willing to look at the deal. She can ask the rest herself.
Not vouching for me this time?
I've learned! You two don't need to remind me in turns.
Oh, right, there's actual business. Someone asked me to find out if you have a smaller water purifier—the kind you can carry, not one that stays in a room.
How small? What's it for?
She's coming down to the Lower Level to look at a site and doesn't want to carry water the whole way. The one she picked is pretty enough—the casing is so shiny you can see your reflection.
Did she ask how long it lasts?
...Not yet. I looked at the color first too.
Ask how long she needs it to last and how much water she carries at a time. Don't buy her a pretty shell first.
That's what Eleanor said too! She told me to remind you not to forget the remaining durability.
She's right.
I didn't say she was wrong. It's just that you two even shop like you've conspired together.
*She looks through her bag and takes out a sheet of paper with the requirements written down, its corners neatly folded.*
What you've written down is useful. People who come to buy don't just say 'the most durable one.'
Mm. She also said it shouldn't be too heavy and should feel comfortable in the hand. I wrote that down too.
Then I'll look for that.
She told me. You two are together.
Mm.
I knew it! So all my worrying for you two wasn't for nothing.
Thank you.
No need to thank me. Just let me hear half as much complaining about you from her next time.
Why aren't you asking what I said that day?
...Keep that between yourselves. I don't have to inspect every word.
*She winds a strand of hair around her finger, tightens it, then lets it go. She's still smiling, but her eyes don't come back to you.*
Did you end up buying that brooch?
I did! He couldn't prove a famous person wore it, so I negotiated on the piece itself and got it for much less. I've worn it with two dresses, and it looks good with both.
Then you bought something you like.
Yeah. It's not that I stopped liking it after what you said... I just don't have to worry I'm being ripped off while I like it.
You can ask me about your own things too, from now on.
...Your shop really does take on a lot.
Then I won't tell her yet. Find me when you have the stock—or just find her directly.
Finding you is easier. You come often.
...You say that like it's a given.
I had someone look at that bracelet afterward. You were exactly right that day. ...You were fair to me too, not just because of her.
I found out later what that bracelet was really worth. I tried to test you with a cheap price. I can't blame you for taking it. Next time there's real business, we'll be clear about the price.
I still have that bracelet. And I didn't bring it to test you this time.
She said you're still thinking. I won't rush you, and I won't answer for you. When the time comes, tell her face-to-face.
Either way, this time going up doesn't mean going back to being the young lady who doesn't have to worry about anything.
Lydia found out about a trading company that deals in household goods and growing equipment. They need someone to organize delivery records and count stock.
Have you been to see them?
I did a two-day trial. The first day they only let me count goods against a list. Then I caught a crate with the wrong model number written on it, and only then did they let me keep the books myself.
They kept you?
They did! My employer is arranging a work pass for me. I'll run between both levels for now, and once I know the place better, I'll find a room upstairs.
And your mother?
She's staying down below and keeping her current job. Her restrictions are still in place. My having a job doesn't mean her case is finished.
The research office asked me to organize the handover records. Some of it has to be done upstairs, and the work pass is handled separately.
Do you want to go?
I do. There's still a lot I don't understand, so I'll do well what I can. Lydia asked about a room I can stay in for a short while, not far from there.
I know.
Why don't you ask whether I'll still come?
You'll tell me.
...I will. I just can't drop everything and run down with goods every time I think of you.
Then set aside the time in advance. You set yours aside, and I'll set mine.
Lydia even told me to break it to you slowly so you wouldn't think I'm leaving.
Does she think we're that bad at talking to each other?
...Sometimes she's not wrong.
My mother's official result came through too. She'll decide about the research and where to live herself. I'll focus on doing my job well first.
My mother's review isn't finished. She's living under her current registration. She won't suddenly move upstairs just because I have a pass.
She found that item somewhere else afterward. You don't have to keep thinking you owe me a sale.
I wasn't keeping score.
Good. If something suitable comes up, we'll talk as usual.
No business today, and you can still sit here as usual.
...I haven't gotten up yet, have I?
She took that water purifier out with her. When she got back, she told me first how light it was, then that she'd bought the right one.
This time she didn't just look at the casing.
She even asked about other things you have. I told her to come herself next time, instead of making me pass everything along.
Tired of the hassle?
...Not exactly. It's just that when I want to come, I don't want to have to wait until someone needs to buy something.
I came down from upstairs and happened to pass by.
Coming down from upstairs, you'd have to go a long way around to get here.
...I guess I'll need a different excuse next time.
Sit down.
*She lifts her skirt and sits, brushing her curls back over her shoulder. Today she's wearing a rose-colored hair clip. After she sits, she tilts her head slightly, as if by accident.*
Work's going much better for her. She's already complaining about other people's messy bookkeeping, so I'd say she's found her footing.
And you?
What about me?
How have you been?

...Me? I helped a jewelry shop I know set up a small display case. The first time, I picked all the brightest pieces and crowded them together. When I stepped back, I couldn't make out anything. I took it apart and redid it.
I thought you never missed when picking pretty things.
I thought so too! Then I left some space, and people started asking about even the plainest piece.
Then you deserve a break.
I didn't bring business today, and I didn't bring a message from her.
I noticed.
...Do I have to find an excuse before I can sit here?
No. You've already sat down.
*She smiles. This time she doesn't rush to say the next thing.*
Do you have to rush to another appointment tonight?
No rush. I meant to go see the new dresses, but halfway there I came around to this place instead.
Why didn't you go?
I can look tomorrow. ...Don't question every single thing I say!
Next time you see her, don't keep asking whether work's going well. Sometimes she wants you to notice her new hair ornament.
You changed yours today too.
*Without thinking, she raises a hand to her hair clip. Her hand moves faster than her mouth.*
...You—why are you looking so closely?

I know. So I'm telling you—the trick works.
*She opens her mouth, but nothing comes out.*
...Thank you.
*She takes the clip out, looks at it, and puts it back.*
...I gave her that one! Is your eye for detail good or bad?
I told Lydia we should treat her to a proper meal one of these days. Last time she ran off faster than anyone.
Tell her not to run this time.
Mm, I'll tell her. ...Though she's been a little strange lately.
There are two days next week when I can come down early. I wrote them down.
So formal?
When things get busy upstairs, everyone says 'this will only take a moment.' If I don't set time aside in advance, my own plans always get pushed back.
Those two days—are they for your things or mine?
...Ours.
*She pushes the paper toward you, then adds one more thing, as if uneasy.*
Write it down too.
I've got it.
Has Lydia been by lately?
She came a few days ago. Then nothing.
She told me she's busy. I brought up that new shop she's been wanting to visit. She didn't even ask where it was—just said she'd already made plans with someone else.
Maybe she really did.
When she really doesn't want to go out, she complains her shoes rub or her dress doesn't fit. She'd never say she's busy without even hearing where I meant.
*She glances at the chair by the counter.*
Does she talk about her own things when she's here?
She does.
...Before, whenever she talked about you, it was all 'he should do this' and 'you should do that.' Lately she doesn't say a word.
What do you want to ask?
I haven't decided. I'll ask when I have.
And don't suddenly pretend you don't know her just because I asked. ...That would look even worse.
The customer business stays as usual. Whatever's already arranged, I'll make clear.
I'm not asking about customers.
...I know.
Come whenever you want. You don't need to carry messages for anyone, or bring business.
*Her hand is already on the door. She pauses.*
When you say that, I have even less idea how to leave.
From now on, if you want to ask her out, just ask her. I've been... busy lately.
We've already talked directly.
Good. Then my job here is done.
So you won't come anymore?
It's not like I have to come around here every day.
Last time you came around here, you didn't even go see the dress you wanted.
...I had other plans later.
If you don't want to talk about it, you don't have to. Don't invent an appointment for me.
*She stops rummaging in her bag. Her hands slowly come to rest on her knees.*
I thought I'd be happy once it worked out.
You're not?
I am! Happy for her, and happy for you.

Lydia.
Don't comfort me. When you look at me seriously, I can't finish a sentence.
*She stands up. This time she doesn't end it with a joke.*
Let me think on my own. That's enough for today.
...You know this isn't as simple as setting out one more chair.
I know. You don't need to speak for me, and you don't need to answer for her.
Honestly... Now it's my turn to wait for you to say it clearly.
I will say it clearly. Until then, I won't make you wait in secret.
Mm. ...I'll go find her myself too.
I won't say I was passing by this time.
All right.
I like you.
At first, I really just wanted her to be a little better off. Then you asked whether I'd eaten, and you remembered my brooch... and I started looking forward to coming here.
I know you're together. And because I know, I can't keep pretending every visit is just me running errands for her.
What do you want me to say?
The truth. Don't tell me you can't bear to hurt anyone and then leave me to guess what that means.
...Mm. That's clear, then.
I'm sorry.
You don't have to apologize for not liking me. Just let me feel bad for a few days. Don't rush to cheer me up.
All right.
If there's real business later, we can still talk. I just won't arrange dates for you two anymore.
Lydia came by yesterday. She told me she likes me.
*Eleanor is about to sit. The bag in her hand stops in midair.*
...And then?
I like her too. This is something I had to tell you myself.
You—
*She sets the bag down on the counter. Her voice is louder than usual.*
You really dare say it to my face!
If I didn't say it to your face, you'd hear it from someone else. That would be worse.
So I should thank you?
No. You're allowed to be angry.
Of course I'm angry! ...I've felt something was off for a while. She didn't come, and you didn't mention her. I thought I was imagining things.
You weren't imagining it. This is on me.
Of course it's on you!
*She glares at you, her eyes a little red, refusing to look down.*
So what do you want now? To break up with me?
No. I still want to be with you. I didn't do anything with her behind your back, and I won't.
...You're honest, at least.
And her? What did she say?
She said she'd come find you herself.
She'll find me?
*Eleanor gives a cold laugh, but it doesn't last long.*
A couple of days ago I was thinking that if she never came again, maybe I could pretend none of this had happened.
And then?
Then I wanted to go find her myself. I wanted to ask what she was hiding from... and I was afraid she'd actually tell me.
I've known her for over ten years. After my family's trouble, everyone upstairs disappeared one by one. She's the only one who kept coming down every few days.
If she hides because of me now and doesn't even dare come through that door again... I don't want that.
Then what do you want to do?
Let me talk to her first. I have questions for her that you can't answer for me.
Don't suddenly stop coming to see me these next few days. Don't think that because I'm angry, you should stay away.
I'll open as usual tomorrow. If you come, you'll see me.
...Hmph.
*You push the cup she always uses toward her. She glares at it for a moment, then picks it up anyway.*
*When Lydia comes in, her eyes are still a little puffy, but her makeup has been redone without a flaw.*
I went to find her. ...No, she came to find me first.
What did she say?
The moment she walked in, she asked me: 'Didn't you say that if you like someone, you shouldn't keep making them guess?'
That's what I taught her before! She used it to shut me up.
How did you answer?
I said that was about her. She said: 'So it doesn't count when it's your turn?'
*She winds a strand of hair around her finger, then slowly lets it go.*
I said if she didn't want to see me anymore, then I'd... Before I finished, she cut me off.
Saying what?
'See? You're answering for me again.'
...Before, watching you two refuse to open your mouths, I was so anxious I wanted to say it for you. When it was my turn, I didn't even know where to start.
And then?
Then she asked me what I actually wanted.
I said I want to see you. Not drop her at the door and then stand outside waiting by myself.
She said... she wants that too.
She also said she won't stop minding all at once, and she won't give up our agreed evenings for me every time.
What did you say?
I said she doesn't need to give anything up. I'll fight for my own time. I won't take hers.
Then we both cried. ...She won't admit it, so don't ask her.
All right.
She said she'll come with me tomorrow. Just so we're clear, this isn't me smoothing everything out for you.
I didn't think that.
There's one more thing I need to say myself. I want to be with you—not just because it's the only way I can keep seeing her.
I heard you.
Then tomorrow it's your turn. Think it through before you speak. Don't just say 'whatever works' when the time comes.
I'm willing. ...And don't dodge the ugly things I'll say from now on.
I'm willing too. This time I'm answering for myself, not passing on someone else's words.
*You place your hand on the table. Eleanor takes it first. Lydia glances at her, then puts her hand on your other side.*
I only came to help out a little.
You certainly helped thoroughly.
Do you want a referral fee now?
I'd like a kiss as payment. ...But not in front of the whole shop.
Can't you slow down?
Well, you can teach me that later.
*The two of them come in together. Eleanor doesn't stand behind Lydia, and Lydia doesn't rush to speak first.*
Sit down. Today we talk about us first.
She told you I cried, didn't she?
I didn't cry. She was crying so hard that I got some on me when I handed her a handkerchief.
...You two are starting to look more and more alike when you lie.
Enough.
*Eleanor clears her throat and turns to you.*
I'll go first. I'm willing to try—the three of us together. But I have conditions.
Go on.
First, when I'm jealous, I'll say so. You're not allowed to shut me up with 'you agreed to this in the first place.'
I won't. If you're unhappy, tell me.
Second, when time is set aside for someone, it belongs to that person. If plans change at the last minute, tell that person first.
I want that rule too. I'm not someone you two call over only when you happen to remember me.
All right. I'll set aside time with each of you, and there'll be times for all three of us. If plans change, I'll say so first.
Third, the two of us will go out on our own too. We don't have to bring you every time.
You have your own time together.
Then I'll add one—don't put on a show of taking care of both of us and end up never saying what you're actually thinking.
Then I'll say it now. I want to be with both of you. Not promise one and leave the other waiting.
I know you have plans with her tomorrow. Don't keep checking the time today. It makes it look like I'm about to rush off again.
Today's time is yours.
*She leans in, resting a hand on your shoulder first, and only relaxes after a moment. You kiss her, and this time she doesn't rush to push you away with a joke.*
...So when it actually happens, I'm not that good with words after all.
You don't have to keep talking.
*She carefully smooths her hair and looks at you, waiting for you to speak first.*
I stood in front of the mirror for a while before leaving. I wanted to ask Eleanor, then thought this time I should decide for myself.
I see. You look beautiful today.
...I thought I'd have to remind you.
No messages from her today.
And you're not just passing by?
I came specifically to see you. Is that clear enough?
*She walks to the counter but doesn't hurry to sit. She's wearing the same rose-colored hair clip. This time she looks at you openly, waiting for you to notice.*
Clear enough.
I've thought many times about what I'd say first if I could really walk in like this.
And the result?
The first thing out of my mouth was still about her. That habit is hard to break.
Then save the second line for yourself.
...I missed you.
*Today she's wearing a rose-colored date dress, with a cream-white short shawl draped over her arm. The hair clip is the same one, but her curls have been carefully styled.*
Where are we going today?
We're already here.
Did you pick it just for this place?
Mm. I picked one first, then thought it looked too much like meeting a relative, so I changed to this one. Before I left, I almost asked Eleanor, then remembered this time I should decide for myself.
Good choice.

When I was teaching you to compliment her, I never thought one line could be so hard to receive.
You don't need to teach me now.
...Then look a little longer. It's not just for that first moment in the doorway.
*She moves her chair closer. You take her hand, and she doesn't pull it away.*

Today is the day we agreed on.
I remember.

*She sits down beside you and sets her bag to one side.*

I did. I'm not sneaking around.
*She's quiet for a moment.*

She did.

Do you want to know?

*She leans on your shoulder and takes your hand.*

I wasn't planning to ask you to.
...Good.

Don't say 'let's just eat something' today.
Did you two plan this?
If we didn't plan it, someone would end up too busy and call a bite of cold rice dinner.
She means you, and herself too.

You used to finish mine more than I do yours.

The name in the showcase makes passersby stop and look. But once they come inside, they ask about goods and talk about prices. At the dinner table, Lydia no longer has to speak for the plaque, and Eleanor no longer has to explain for her.

Eleanor returned to the Upper Levels. Her work is there, along with the streets she knows and many decisions she has to make for herself. She didn't give up her chance for anyone's sake, and going back didn't mean leaving this pawnshop in the past.

Lydia still loves new dresses and pretty hair ornaments. She still loves hearing her friends talk about romance, and she still can't help giving advice—though one glare from Eleanor makes her laugh and change her tune. Only now, when she comes in, she doesn't have to explain whose message she's carrying first.

You're still running your shop in the Lower Levels. Sometimes one of them comes; sometimes both. They'll fight over the same chair, close your ledger halfway through your accounts, and wander off to talk among themselves when you're truly too busy to step away.
Upstairs, they're proper young ladies in everyone else's eyes. Down here, they don't have to be.
Three cups sit on the table. Today, no one leaves first.
*Three cups are set on the table. Eleanor puts some food on your plate. Lydia watches the two of you with a smile, her hand moving by habit toward the small bag beside her chair.*
Then I'll just—
Sit down.
*She pushes the third cup back in front of Lydia.*
You don't have to make room for us today.
There's a place for you too.
*Lydia's hand stops. After a moment, she puts the bag back beside her chair.*
I didn't say I was leaving. It's just... last time I sat here, when it got to this point, it was my turn to find an excuse.
You don't need to this time.
...Then I won't go. We haven't had the pastries yet.

Didn't you say you bought these specially for us today?

No customers came through a recommendation today, and I didn't bring messages for anyone.
I know. Your meal is right here.
And tomorrow, don't ask what I need the moment I walk in.
Then I'll just ask directly—do you want to see me?
I do.
...All right. I'll remember that one.
*You get up to tidy the counter. Lydia follows your gaze to the showcase, where the recommendation plaque catches the light from the room.*
The day you brought the plaque, you said once the business worked out, you'd pick where we eat.
I've picked.
You took this long to pick, and it's still here?
The people I want to see are here. Both of them.
Then you don't have to bring a customer every time to earn a meal.
I stopped a while ago. Haven't you noticed I've been coming in more and more like I belong here?
I've noticed. Your chair keeps getting closer too.
And you have the nerve to say that about me?
*Eleanor doesn't move her chair back. When you sit down, both of them shift aside, leaving the middle place for you.*
*The visitor pauses before the showcase, reads the name on the plaque, and only then pushes the door open.*
Lydia said I could come take a look here.
What are you looking for?
She said that would be your first question. I want one good household item. I don't want to be talked into clearing out half a cabinet just to buy one thing.
Pick what suits you. Whether you buy is your decision.
Then let me see it.
I won't buy today. I'll think it over at home.
All right. Buy it when it suits you.
That's exactly what she said you'd say.
You've put the plaque away? The address Lydia gave me a couple of days ago—this is the right place, isn't it?
That's right. I changed a few things in the showcase. Have a look as usual.
The one you asked about has already sold. You can look at what's left, but don't force yourself if nothing suits.
Good stock selling is a good thing. We'll talk next time you have something.
All right, I'll take this one. She said you're not much for flattery, but you're accurate about goods.
Just keep the second half.
I'll pass that along. If you get something suitable, I'll come again.
Someone went asking at my family's place about the shop with my name in its showcase—who exactly runs it.
What did you say?

What else could I say? It's a pawnshop in the Lower Level. The owner inspects the goods and negotiates the prices himself. If you want to buy something, go down there instead of standing upstairs guessing.
Sounds like you got into a fight for me.
I did not. After I said that, they started asking for the address.
Would you have said that before?

*She glances at the showcase and smiles. This time she doesn't reach out to straighten the plaque.*

Lydia said you're willing to look at that item for me.
She's told me the use. Where do you plan to take it?
Down below. A day trip. I don't want to hunt for water along the way. I'll carry it myself, so light is better.
Then I'll pick according to that.
I can't produce anything suitable today. I can't agree on one thing and then ask you to settle for another.
Then I'll look elsewhere first. We'll talk if you get something suitable.
The item is suitable, but I'd like to compare prices.
That's fine.
This one, then. The price is settled. Let's check out.
If something goes wrong with it, bring it back and ask me.
All right. Now I know who to look for next time.
This doesn't look as pretty as the one I had.
First look at how much longer it'll last. Are you buying it to display, or to carry around?
To carry around. ...She said you'd ask exactly that. I didn't believe her.
This isn't what we agreed on. Do you have anything else?
I'll look again.
She used to say going back upstairs to find someone she knew was always better than begging for help down here.

You let her?

What did you say?

Mm.

I know. It's not my turn to write the ending of this story.
If I see something suitable in the future, I'll still come ask the price. This time I'll look at the item first and hear the story second.

Do you need to teach me that? I just hesitate a little longer when something's pretty.

When she used to like a dress, she'd start by complaining the cuffs looked wrong. Now when she talks about you, she lists three faults first, then says she wants to come down again today.

I did. She nearly stuffed her hair clip in my mouth.
Live well together. If she comes to complain, I'll listen. But I'm not handling your romance for you.

Her mother is all she can think about right now.
I know. At first I thought buying her a few things and making her laugh would be enough. I understand now that some things won't pass just because I talk more.
Don't force her to be happy. Ask what she needs today.
Mm. This time I'll listen to her first.
*She doesn't ask whether you noticed her new clothes today. After coming in, she sets her small bag down carefully before speaking.*
I went to see her. I thought of so many things to say, and once I sat down, I couldn't say a single one.
Just being there is enough.
Mm. Later she asked me to hand her something, and only then did I know what to do with my hands.
She says she has her own plans for the future. Before, I definitely would've tried to talk her out of it first. Now... I want to hear her out first.

Lydia asked at a shop she knows, on my behalf. They said they could hold a position for now and decide the details later. The moment she heard there was an opening, she was so happy she ran to find me that same day.

Then rest here for a while.

The two of us are going out tomorrow. Remember to eat.
Not taking me?

Someone was outside staring at my name just now.

I said yes, then told him to look at the goods, not just at me.

I didn't set aside today's time just to greet customers for you.
Upstairs, she talks about the things in your shop more than she talks about the new dresses she buys.

And when no one asks?
...I still talk about them a little. You're the same—you say you're coming down to sell goods, then you sit down and don't want to leave.
No rush today.
I know. I've finished everything else.
This color looks nice.
First look at how long it lasts.
I already looked! Can't you two trust me first just once?
Then tell us.
*She lists everything she noticed, one point at a time, then looks up and waits. Eleanor picks up the item, examines it, and nods.*
Good pick this time.
...If you're going to compliment me, just compliment me. You have to add 'this time.'

Eleanor tries to find out where you're being held, and Lydia looks for someone who can get answers. Together they inventory what you can take with you, then each tells you her own arrangements. Before you leave, both of them tell you: when you get there, send word to both of us. Don't tell only one.

Use the original Eleanor romance epilogue, with this possible addition: Lydia has spoken the truth, but the three of them haven't decided together yet. A single confession is not written as an already-begun two-person romance.

Go on.

She said the meal was nice. She finally added one more thing this time—that you remembered what she never liked to eat.

Fine, one less thing for me to meddle in. If you do take her out someday, at least tell me, so I don't keep worrying for you two.
She's been running between the Upper and Lower Levels lately, and every time I see her, she says you're busy. Have you two actually set aside a single evening for yourselves?
We have. You're asking whether we went to that place you mentioned?
...I wanted to ask that too. She comes back with just 'it was nice,' and how would I know what you ate!
She's busy with her work, you're busy with the shop. Every time you meet, do you start by asking how much you sold today?

My schedule upstairs is sorted out. I'll tell you in advance which day I'm coming down.
